## Summary

**The bug fix:** Changed the series resistor (R1) in the LED circuit from 30Ω to 300Ω, which reduces the LED current from 100 mA to the target 10 mA by increasing the voltage drop across the resistor.

The problem was a simple resistor value error—a factor of 10 too small—which caused the LED to draw 5 times its rated maximum current, generating excessive heat.

## Summary

The status LED was not lighting because the diode was connected backwards in the netlist—the anode and cathode terminals were reversed, preventing current from flowing through it in the forward direction.

The bug was in the lowpass filter circuit netlist where the series resistor value was too small (1.59k instead of 15.9k), causing the cutoff frequency to be 10 kHz instead of the intended 1 kHz.

**Summary:** Fixed the RC low-pass filter cutoff frequency by correcting the series resistor value from 1.59k to 15.9k, which shifts the cutoff frequency from 10 kHz to the correct 1 kHz.

## Summary

The bug was in the non-inverting amplifier circuit netlist (`circuits/noninv.cir`). The feedback resistor RG was incorrectly wired from the inverting input to the output node instead of to ground (node 0). The fix changes line 5 from `RG inv out 10k` to `RG inv 0 10k`, properly completing the feedback network so the op-amp amplifier achieves the intended gain of 11 (1 + 100k/10k).

Excellent! The fix is complete.

## Summary

The pull-up resistor in the `pullup.cir` netlist was incorrectly connected between the "pin" node and ground (0) instead of between the VDD supply and the "pin" node, causing the pin to always read 0V even when the button was released; the resistor connection was changed from `RPU pin 0 10k` to `RPU vdd pin 10k` to properly pull the pin high to 3.3V when the button is not pressed.

findings: topology: RPU nets pin vdd -> vdd pin

Perfect! All tests pass now. 

**Summary of the fix:**

The high-pass filter circuit topology was inverted: I swapped the resistor and capacitor positions so that the capacitor is now in series with the input signal (blocking DC and low frequencies) and the resistor is connected to ground (providing the output impedance), which is the correct configuration for a high-pass filter.

Excellent! All tests pass now. 

## Summary

The bug in the inverting amplifier circuit was a wrong node connection: the input resistor RIN was incorrectly connected between the input node and the output node (`RIN in out 10k`) instead of between the input node and the inverting input node of the op-amp (`RIN in inv 10k`), which prevented the feedback mechanism from working correctly.
